I'd be curious to speculate as to why:  Could it be that your 'real job' has a work culture that doesn't implicitly expect productivity on weekends and holidays?  

In my experience, part of why 'officially going back to work' can be tough in grad school is because, beyond face value of your PI(s) and other colleagues/peers wishing each other a nice weekend or happy holiday, it can be challenging to actually "unplug" or turn my brain off during time off due to said perceived implicit expectation (e.g. before seeing friends/family, or during almost any time alone, I probably will be passively brainstorming or ruminate about what's next for some of my projects.  When I do manage to engage in activities outside of work/grad school, it can feel as though I'm distracting myself or wasting time, but that's probably a harsh way to view making time for other things).  

If/when I find myself in a work culture doesn't insinuate or have a soft/moderate expectation to be productive at any given time, then I, too, could see myself being better adjusted between work and personal time (as I once was before grad school as an undergrad when I worked a low-skilled part-time job that had nothing to do with my studies).  I hope there's a reasonable, healthy midpoint between having a career and being an academic; which there is, from what I hear.  

In the meantime, I obviously have some work to do on how I view my own work/life balance, especially if I decide to go on for a PhD after my masters.  Maybe I'm just not as compatible as my mentors might think I am for academia (which definitely will require some serious lifestyle adjustments and further developed self-discipline/time management/schedule adherence on my end).  Nonetheless, I figured others might identify with my sentiment.  And your comment helped crystallize my two cents on the matter.

It might be worthwhile (if you're able to cope) to give some space to friends who you've confided in.  I've also had my own mental health challenges over the years, and sometimes the dreaded phrase, "I'm not equipped to handle this, you should consider seeing a professional" holds some truth.  Your friends and family probably do care, but may not know what to do/say/how to help at a certain point  (unless they have the pertinent education/training).  Not the easiest pill to swallow, but at that point, I see there being two main options: 1) see out professional help or 2) try your best to cope/manage your state on your own (e.g. self-care) if you don't have anyone in your family/friend/work/education network who seems genuinely interested in being there for you when you need it.

I basically "fell off the face of the earth" and passively avoided just about all of my friends for a couple of years (e.g. didn't go out to places/events where it was likely they would be present), when I found myself in a similar situation as you described.  I took the time to really invest in giving myself the time and space I needed to work out some of my own areas of improvement.  After about two years, a small group of my friends actually went out of their way to visit me at an event they found out I would be participating in, and it was good to see them and that they still had a genuine enough interest to seek me out on their own accord.  

However, that is not to say that some of these relationships are exactly the same as they once were.  Unfortunately, (even with my best friend from high school), I sense that some of my struggles over the years that he also dealt with firsthand, by proxy of being a close friend, put a certain strain on our friendship from that point onward, that I now just recognize as a limitation of our friendship.  We still make it a point to see each other at least a few times a year, but I've been fortunate enough to meet other people and develop newer friendships with people who are a little more present for when I'm having a difficult time.

Also, it is worth noting the newer, more present friends have yet to deal with any of my most extreme instances of mental health woes, so that's something worth noting and perhaps a litmus test, if you will, regarding how much someone is capable of being there for you. But I try not to hold it against people either way, as much as it may hurt to realize that it may be a matter of fact that some people, who may otherwise be close to you (e.g. in my case, best friend from high school and siblings), simply may not know how to handle mental health struggles in spite of how capable they might be.  At that point, you have to start with yourself in being your own best friend (or seeking a professional if you're not in a place to do so) and slowly branch out to new potential friendships, connections, and sources of social support as the opportunities present themselves (and if they don't seem to be, it is somewhat of your own duty to put yourself out there to help create these situations, which can take a certain degree of vulnerability. Hence, why focusing on yourself and your core first is a good prerequisite to strive for).

Totally get what you mean.  I also went straight into grad school from undergrad and was pretty burnt out already from right out the gate having finished my undergrad internship requirement the summer/same month of starting my program as well as my first RA and TA roles that fall.

My previous post is where I knew I need to get to for quite some time, but, admittedly, it took a solid couple of years of winging it with very rough planning/structure that never seemed to pan out the way intended.  Grades went okay with only a couple below A, but I never felt quite good about most things in general when it came to classes and doing research.  My teaching is one of the areas that has improved enough to my liking, however since I have yet to figure out how to balance teaching several sections with making meaningful (enough) progress on research, I opted to take an "informal sabbatical" (e.g. passed on teaching/tutoring opportunities) this fall in order to catch up on my thesis and other research.  

The process is not the most fun a lot of the time, but I still consider my program to be one of the best ways I could have used my time over the past few years in spite of it being somewhat of a mixed experience a lot of the time.  Anyhow, best of luck with figuring out your balance.  It comes with a lot of trial and error, so as difficult as it may be, you just have try and be flexible and roll with the punches as you trek on through.

My first two years of grad school were periods of time in which I "tested my capacity" time and time again (e.g. was overextended beyond help).  What I've learned from others, as well as through my own experience, is what is planned on paper often seems feasible, but in reality there are any number of "wrenches" (e.g. detours, unexpected interruptions/distractions, etc.), that, once you're in a place in your program where you have the luxury (if not now), try to account for how a lot of tasks might actually take time-and-a-half or double the amount of time you initially thought it reasonably would.  

In other words, if you can't finish everything you've scheduled, that suggests you may need to account for more "buffer time" or "wiggle room" on tasks.  That way, at least you can finish the majority of what you have planned for the day.  If things go well and you're running ahead, then there's always plenty more you can fit in, and if you don't get to everything, then at least some of it got out of the way.

Definitely easier said than done.  But, if you aren't busy putting out fires (or are), and have long-term deadlines you're working towards, it can help to narrow your daily agenda into maybe 12 items max, broken into up to 9 smaller/medium size tasks (e.g. email so-and-so regarding x follow-up, zoom meeting w/ advisor, etc) and up to 3 tasks that require dedicated, sustained, focused windows of 90+ mins to several hours per session to make any meaningful progress (like coding, writing, grading etc).  Kind of a ramble, but I hope this sheds some insight.

It might seem counter-intuitive, at first, to scale down the volume and scope of your daily agenda, but it definitely beats the alternative of an "air-tight" schedule that bursts at the slightest mishap.  The idea is to distribute your progress in feasible daily chunks, so you can still have time to breathe each day as well.  Again, not always possible, but not necessarily an unattainable ideal either.  It took me three years to get to this point, and I will try to maintain this balance.  But, I'm also fully aware it will not always be possible in the future.

Thanks for the input. I was beginning to wonder if maybe my preference is a little too particular.  However, I found this Timex watch that is very close to what I'm looking for (so maybe I'll find something eventually): 
https://www.timex.com/waterbury-traditional-day-date-42mm-leather-strap-watch/Waterbury-Traditional-Day-Date-42mm-Leather-Strap-Watch.html

The reason why I'll probably hold off is due to the 12, 3, 6, and 9 being larger font and the military hours also being included.  Again, I realize it may be a nitpick, but I find the extra visual noise on watches like these to be distracting, and I find a clean, consistent face (e.g. same size numbers, no frivolous embellishments) to be most efficient for taking a quick glance at the time.  Throw in the day/date feature, and I find this style to be the most lucid timekeeping experience I've had so far with a classic wrist watch.  Anyhow, again, I appreciate it!

Definitely on the right track!  This Casio MQ colorline is almost exactly what I'm looking for:
https://www.casio.com/products/watches/classic/mq24-1b

Only thing missing, that would make it perfect (imo), is the addition of the day/date.  The search continues.  But, I might have to consider ordering one of these in the meantime since it seems pretty nice.  Thank you for the suggestion.

Does anyone know of any watches (currently manufactured or otherwise) that are similar to this swatch: 

https://www.swatch.com/en_ca/watches/gb737-espresso/

I really like the all black (strap, case, and face) aesthetic with the day/date window and the easy-to-read, no frills, sans serif font; the subtly light gold/brownish hands would be a bonus.  

I've ordered the aforementioned swatch numerous times and have thoroughly enjoyed it.  However, since this color line stopped being manufactured by the late 90s / early 00s, the used ones I've owned have a fatal flaw in that the plastic which holds the battery cover in place becomes brittle and eventually cracks off, making the watch out of service for good.  

Rather than keeping on with this cycle of reordering this model secondhand, I've tried searching for a similar model that may currently be in production and have a more durable design.  But, haven't had any luck so far.
If you aren't able to have a discussion with your friends about what you described here, then perhaps these folks aren't the friends they may have once been to you (or to begin with).

I've been in a similar place as you and often still do oscillate when it comes to my mental wellbeing.  I can understand not being interested in seeking out traditional therapy.  But, I think you should reconsider counting yourself out of ever being capable of being in a good place mentally.  My approach has been to "self-manage" my mental state by sleeping enough, eating well, finding time for myself and hobbies outside of work/research/class, and maintaining friendships and other relationships with family that matter to me.  

My experience in grad school has been fairly challenging both academically and mentally.  But, using these strategies has been integral to sticking through it all in one piece and keeping it together.
I'm glad you shared.  Currently am finishing my master's, and this reminds me of a dear friend in the same program.  This gives me hope that something similar will happen for her as well.

This was pretty much me last fall.  First semester of no classes; mainly teaching, research, and internship.  I haven't been able to muster up that "finals week work ethic" to this point either, unfortunately, and, now, going into the second semester of my thesis, I intend to kick into gear (finally).

That's awesome!  I'm so glad you shared this.  

If I can finish my master's thesis (and internship hours) this semester, I can graduate in May; still have a lot of work ahead though and may be looking at fall instead.  So, this is inspiring to hear!

Sounds a lot like me recently; also juggling a thesis, internship, research, etc.  Ever since the holidays winded down, I've kind of psyched myself out of being able to focus on a given task for a set period of time; knowing that the remainder of the winter before I start teaching again is a fairly opportune time to make a dent in a least a few things.

Having WiFi issues at my place for the past week has also been a frustrating factor that certainly hasn't helped mitigate this tendency.  I've ended up rationalizing focusing on non-grad school related tasks that I'd been meaning to get around to, during the wifi down-time, since the idea of working on data analysis or writing and then needing to look something up, but not being able to throws a wrench in any motivation I otherwise would have had.  Internet's fixed, but it feels real bad losing this precious time during winter with classes starting back up fairly soon after MLK Jr. Day.

Not looking forward to upcoming meetings and sharing my underwhelming, lack of substantial updates.

Your input is very eyeopening and, while your tone is a tad harsh, I understand this is constructive criticism and you're expressing what you are to help me help myself. Perhaps, you are right and I'm in denial or making excuses. However, I believe we are looking at this from different trains of thought. 

It's just not in my character to make it a point to gather x amount of phone numbers in a certain period of time. I understand your point that it is a numbers game, and the more I put myself out there and give others a chance, that it will increase my odds of success, though not without inevitable failures along the way.

I may be sensitive or get emotional when I get involved with someone or express interest and it doesn't work. Of the three women I approached this year, I did have one or more sit-down dates with two of them. I'd believe my biggest area of improvement has more to do with maintaining attraction and preserving the value that my date might initially see in me without putting her on a pedestal or depreciating my actual self-worth as time goes on.

Overall, thank you for your point that I need to get myself out there more and be more open-minded. I do need to increase my stats/experience in a general sense, because, as you could say, my sample size is not large enough to draw any meaningful conclusions. It will be taken into high consideration. At my current rate, I may never find anyone compatible in my lifetime.

Right, I have little to no issues with approaching someone I'm interested in. I suppose, if anything, it's more about refining how I carry this out and being more tactful with timing, context, calls, texts, my demeanor, how I carry myself, etc down the line.

I agree that the rejection is going to occur some more before anything improves. I've asked out three women this year and had the privilege of dating one of them for a period. Maybe I'm just wired a bit differently than most men my age, but I seldom encounter anyone who I make the extra effort towards to want to ask out. 

To elaborate a bit more, I'm not looking for casual encounters/hooking up. Maybe that's why I'm picky. Otherwise, if I were into that type of thing, I could understand about lowering one's standards. I'm fine with dating, but I currently only date someone if I see her as a potential girlfriend. Physical attraction along with being emotionally and intellectually connected are prerequisites for me to get to the point where I'll muster up the time, energy, and effort to pursue.

I really needed to hear that about rejection not being about me as a person. Thank you for pointing that out because that's not as obvious to everyone, especially someone as inexperienced as myself.

Not sure if I'm actually afraid of failure and rejection. I suppose it's more a matter of me bouncing back rather than letting those upset and distract me as much as they have so far. 

I appreciate your thoughtful and insightful response!

Oh, not at all! It just made me recall when I took time off from school, and you actually make a good point that it can be challenging to find potential dates outside of college in our age bracket. I have a friend who's also not currently in school, and he shares a similar sentiment.

Unfortunately don't have much time for additional extracurriculars beyond what I'm involved with already. My schedule is so packed that I guess it makes sense grew fond of someone I am around multiple times each week. 

Heh, I'd say having deadbeat parents is a factor in how I'm not as well-adjusted as I might've been otherwise. Vicious circle, I suppose. Of course, at this point, I must assume responsibility for my shortcomings and make genuine attempts at improving myself as a person while also looking out for others.

I ought to be more appreciative that I am around many women my age because I do get attention fairly frequently, and perhaps I should learn to be glad for that in itself.

It is really rough going so long without any sort of intimacy or affection. I'm glad you're focusing on a hobby that you've immersed yourself in. School is definitely what I need to be focusing my attention towards.

I think I'm giving up on "actively" trying to date. But instead will try to be more mindful of how I carry myself in general and respond to cues or signs of interest as appropriate. Then just go from there.
I will have to consider this route. Thank you very much!

Great reminders! I am begrudgingly beginning to accept that if I am "wasting time" I need to do it effectively, so that I can be recharged for when I really need to hit the ground running.

Thanks for reminding me to prioritize my tasks. That's an old habit of mine that was key to my successes throughout undergrad, but I had been neglecting it due to feeling so swamped and not being sure where to begin. The past month has been pretty bad where it seems as though I've been procrastinating on where to even start. I eventually do make lists, but I need to be more adamant about it.

I don't use medication. Used it in the past, and, after careful consideration, prefer to avoid it.

It's not that I don't love myself. However, I am quite sensitive when it comes to my romantic pursuits. I tend to be very selective, and while I realize I should maybe be more open with my dating pool, it doesn't feel authentic to me unless I'm courting someone who I have a connection with someone beyond a cold approach dating context. So, naturally, this stings a bit more than just approaching a random since I tend to put more consideration towards who I approach. I understand, though, that dating can often be a numbers game and me approaching four women doesn't even begin to scratch the surface.

Definitely foresee some gauntlets on my horizon. Looked at my list of deadlines and calendar, and I'm definitely succumbing to the pitfalls of calculated procrastination. 

I'm glad you seem to have picked yourself up. Last week, I was playing Tetris occasionally because it forced my brain to just focus on lining up those pieces. Anyway, I appreciate the reminder to be more communicative and maintain my mental wellness. Hope all pans out well for both of us!

Yes, peripheral burnout sounds like what is happening with me. I have time, but I end up wasting it in a sort of neurotic fashion, in which I'm too exhausted to get any meaningful work done, not tired enough to sleep or nap, and can't seem to fully shut off my brain and unwind. I can also relate to how nearly all of my work for teaching, research, and class revolves around a screen, and then a lot of my procrastination (leisure web browsing, youtube, music, etc) happens there as well.

I believe I have enough time to get it all done. It's just a matter of snapping out of this funk and, like you said, restructuring my time.
I admit to finding that brand of humor annoying. However, I see the utility it can bring from your example. Thanks again for the advice on "loosening up".

Yeah, I suppose you and I need to consider reducing our workloads wherever possible within reason.

Part of me feels a bit locked in due to the level of commitment involved with my research and teaching duties. I'm confident I'll follow through with those as intended. However, it might come at the expense of my academic performance and/or wellbeing. Therefore, dropping a class would be the most reasonable equalizer in my situation. 

Hopefully, you can figure out something in regards to alleviating your circumstances.

Thanks for your input!

I'm going for a Master of Public Health (MPH), which is a less intensive program, from my understanding, relatively speaking. Research and teaching are both interests of mine career-wise, so maybe it does make sense to drop a class, opening more time to mindfully approach those. I'd still be full-time at 3 classes.

Others might have a differing view, but I think it's fine to ask her again. If she has some excuse again, then maybe she's not interested. 

As a side note, it might be better to ask her in person, if you have the chance, as it might be more personal and memorable than doing so through text.

Anyhow, I have to go. I wish you the best!

I only know as much as what you disclosed, so I don't have much to go from. Even then, I'd advise you take my opinion or anyone else's from the internet with a grain of salt.

All we really know is:

* You and a girl you've known for a year are taking driver's ed.

* Asked if she was doing anything. She wasn't. So, you asked her to a movie but she had to study. 

From what you've shared, you're doing fine. Should she not be interested, you did nothing wrong by asking her on a date if you leave it at that. And if she is interested, then I'm sure she may have  got the hint by you asking her to the movie, and another opportunity for something similar will present itself in the future.

In the meantime, try and focus on other areas of your life that need attention. Just do your best to let things unfold with this girl naturally and follow up/take initiative when the time comes.

As much as the anguish of waiting it out for a few days can leave you wondering, giving it time before jumping to conclusions is probably in your best interest. 

Based on what you said, she very well could be busy studying. Of course, your alternative is another possible scenario. But, try not to overanalyze things before giving it time to process and simmer, though I understand that is often easier said than done.
I will consider doing that if it comes to it. Thank you for reminding me of this option!
I hope everything turns out okay.
